A good tool holder makes the tools easy to see, identify, remove and return. It should remain stable while it is being used and make a missing tool obvious.

<div class="ter-process-flow ter-process-flow--strong" aria-label="Organizer design cycle"><span>DESIGN</span><span>BUILD</span><span>FEEDBACK</span><span>REVISION</span></div>

## What makes a good tool holder?

| Design criterion | What a student should be able to show |
|---|---|
| **Visible inventory** | Every tool or part has a visible position. A missing item can be noticed quickly. |
| **Clear labels** | Names, sizes, outlines or colour-independent symbols show where each item belongs. |
| **Easy access** | A user can see the handle, grip it and remove or return the tool without moving neighbouring tools. |
| **Secure fit** | The holder supports the tool without being so tight that normal removal becomes difficult. Sharp or fragile parts are protected. |
| **Freestanding stability** | The holder stands on its own and does not tip when a tool is removed from an outside position. |
| **Wall option** | The design can include a tested wall interface, such as a French cleat, while still allowing safe removal or service. Mounting hardware must suit the actual wall and load. |
| **Stacking or modularity** | Modules can align, connect or stack without hiding labels, blocking tools or becoming unstable. |
| **Simple construction** | Parts, joints and fasteners are understandable, buildable and replaceable. |

Not every holder needs every feature. The designer chooses the criteria that matter for the tools, user and location, then tests those claims.

## A practical test

1. **Glance test:** Can another student identify every tool and notice what is missing?
2. **Reach test:** Can the user remove and return each tool with a natural grip?
3. **Tip test:** Does the organizer remain stable when the heaviest outside tool is removed?
4. **Mount test:** If it hangs, can it be attached, removed and loaded without pulling away or rotating?
5. **Module test:** If it stacks or connects, do the modules remain aligned and usable?

Record the result of each test. A claim such as “wall-mountable” or “stackable” is not complete until the actual interface has been built and tested.

## From measurements to a prototype

1. Compare the examples and decide which features fit the real tools and user.
2. Measure the real tools, including handles, collars, tapers and the hand clearance needed for removal.
3. Draw the concept using orthographic views and an isometric or assembly view.
4. Use the [Fabrication Plate Builder](../plate-builder/index.qmd) for plates, rings and repeated holder holes.
5. Use the [Laser-Cut Leg & Support Builder](../leg-builder/index.qmd) when the organizer needs a freestanding base, legs or a rear support.
6. Find calibration files and reusable geometry in [Laser-Cutting Files and Resources](../../../teaching-materials/laser-cutting/index.qmd).
7. Make a small fit test before building the complete prototype.
8. Photograph the build, collect feedback and record the next revision.

## Grade 9 knife-holder example

::: {.ter-case-status}
**TIJ1OR-E Knife Holder Design · Revision 2 · March 22, 2024**

**Orthographic drawing exists · publishable site copy pending · project photos pending**

This was a Grade 9 project, not a perfect final answer. It is useful because students can compare the drawing with a real fabricated object and decide which features should be kept or improved. The original orthographic and actual project photos will be added when publishable copies are available. No substitute image has been invented.
:::

<div class="ter-case-study-grid">
<section>

### What the example already demonstrates

- individual, visible positions for the knives or tools;
- quick visual counting and easy access;
- a freestanding angled form;
- simple wood, screw and rope construction;
- orthographic and isometric views that communicate the intended build.

### Drawing facts

- drawing title: **TIJ1OR-E Knife Holder Design**;
- units: inches;
- identified materials: wood, screws and rope;
- projecting supports or nails: approximately **2 in spacing**;
- projecting length: approximately **2 in**;
- insertion: approximately **1/2 in**;
- angle: approximately **35°**.

</section>
<section>

### What a later revision could improve

- add clear labels or silhouettes so every part has an obvious home;
- show the complete inventory at a glance;
- add a removable wall-mounting option;
- create repeatable interfaces so modules can be placed side by side or stacked;
- preserve the stable freestanding option;
- test one-handed removal, tipping and neighbouring-tool clearance.

The useful strengths of Revision 2 should remain visible in the next concept. A later design does not need to change everything.

</section>
</div>

### Media to add from the real project

| Evidence | Purpose | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Orthographic drawing with front, top and side views | Shows dimensions and intended construction | Original exists; publishable copy needed |
| Isometric or assembly view | Shows how the parts fit together | Confirm with the original drawing set |
| Front photo with all tools in place | Shows visibility, labels and inventory | Photo needed |
| Side photo | Shows the angle, footprint and freestanding stability | Photo needed |
| Rear or mounting-detail photo | Shows whether a wall interface exists or could be added | Photo needed |
| Empty-holder photo | Makes each labelled storage position visible | Photo needed |

## Add a future build

Each case study should include a finished photo, original drawing, problem, key dimensions, materials, fabrication method, what worked, feedback, next revision, downloads where appropriate and a clear validation status.

Do not mark a design “validated” merely because a file renders or a digital assembly looks plausible. Distinguish **drawing available**, **dimension-tested**, **fit-tested**, **shop-tested** and **photo documented**. If evidence is missing, say so instead of filling the gap with a stock or generated image.
